procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 12.11.2020 passed by the learned CJM dismissing the application filed by the original complainant (respondent no. 1) under Section 156(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.).
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The original complainant (respondent no. 1) filed a Criminal Revision Application No. 92/2021 before the High Court of Calcutta challenging the CJM's order. The High Court allowed the revision application, quashed and set aside the CJM's order dated 12.11.2020, and remanded the matter to the CJM to reconsider the application under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. in light of the High Court's observations and pass a reasoned order.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The original respondents (alleged accused) filed the present appeals before the Supreme Court, feeling aggrieved and dissatisfied with the High Court's judgment and order. They challenged the High Court's decision to quash the CJM's order and remand the matter.

directions: While affirming the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court remanding the matter back to the Magistrate, the subsequent order passed by the Magistrate on remand, pursuant to the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court is set aside and the matter is remitted back to the Magistrate.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate, at the stage of deciding an application under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C., is justified in verifying the truth and veracity of the allegations, or is the inquiry limited to whether the allegations disclose the commission of a cognizable offence?

facts: A victim-complainant filed an application under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. before a Magistrate, seeking a direction for the police to register an FIR for the offence of rape.
The Magistrate initially dismissed the application, and on revision, the High Court set aside the Magistrate's order.
The High Court held that a Magistrate, at the stage of a 156(3) application, could not verify the veracity of the allegations and remitted the matter back for reconsideration.
The core legal issue before the Supreme Court was to determine the scope of the Magistrate's inquiry at the pre-cognizance stage under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C.
law: Section 156(3) of the Cr.P.C. empowers a Magistrate to order a police investigation into a cognizable offence before taking cognizance.

The Supreme Court considered its previous rulings in *Lalita Kumari*, which holds that if a complaint discloses a cognizable offence, the police must register an FIR and cannot conduct a preliminary inquiry into the veracity of the allegations (except in certain specified cases).
The Court also considered its decision in *Priyanka Srivastava*, which states that a Magistrate must apply a judicious mind when considering a 156(3) application.

The Court sought to harmonize the principles, clarifying that there should not be a mismatch between the duty of a police officer under Section 154(1) and the jurisdiction of a Magistrate under Section 156(3).
application: The Supreme Court held that the Magistrate's primary role at the Section 156(3) stage is to determine if the allegations in the complaint disclose the commission of a cognizable offence.
The Court explicitly stated that it is "impermissible and contrary to law" for the Magistrate to adjudicate on the merits of the allegations or determine the facts as baseless at this stage.

If the Magistrate is satisfied that a cognizable offence is disclosed, they "must stay his hands, direct registration of an FIR and leave it to the investigative agency to unearth the facts and ascertain the truth of the allegations."

The application of "judicial mind" by the Magistrate does not extend to verifying the truthfulness of the complaint. Instead, it involves exercising discretion on the future course of action, which includes:
1. Directing the registration of an FIR under Section 156(3).
2. Taking cognizance of the offence and proceeding under Section 202 Cr.P.C.
3. For good reasons, directing a preliminary inquiry by the police, in line with the *Lalita Kumari* judgment.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition that a Magistrate is justified in verifying the truth and veracity of allegations while deciding an application under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. The Court concluded that the Magistrate's inquiry is limited to ascertaining whether the complaint discloses the commission of a cognizable offence. If it does, the matter should be sent for police investigation, as it is the role of the investigative agency, not the Magistrate at the pre-cognizance stage, to determine the truth of the allegations.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate, at the stage of deciding an application under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C., is justified in verifying the truth and veracity of the allegations, or is the inquiry limited to whether the allegations disclose the commission of a cognizable offence?
appellant_arguments: The High Court erred in quashing the well-reasoned order of the Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) who had dismissed the complaint under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C.

The CJM was justified in making pertinent observations and giving cogent reasons for dismissing the application, such as noting the inordinate delay in making the police complaint, which implies a Magistrate can look into the veracity of the allegations.
respondent_arguments: The scope of a Magistrate's inquiry under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. is limited.

Based on a harmonious reading of Supreme Court precedents (Lalita Kumari and Priyanka Srivastava), the Magistrate's role is only to determine if the allegations disclose the commission of a cognizable offence, not to verify the truth of the allegations.

cases.principle: Mandatory nature of Section 154(1) of the Code.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Subject to the broad guidelines available from the scheme of the Code, the exercise of discretion by the Magistrate is guided by the interest of justice from case to case.
obiter: If a learned Single Judge of the High Court is of the opinion that the view taken in a case by a co-ordinate Bench is not correct law, propriety demands that the learned Single Judge ought to refer the matter to a larger Bench, rather than taking a contrary view.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: At the stage of deciding an application under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C., the Magistrate's inquiry is limited to determining if the allegations disclose the commission of a cognizable offence. It is impermissible and contrary to law for the Magistrate to conduct an adjudication on the merits of the allegations or to determine the facts as baseless without further scrutiny and examination, as the power under this section is very limited and does not travel into the arena of the merits of the case.
legal_tests_applied: The legal test for a Magistrate under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. is to determine whether the facts and circumstances of the case, based on the relevant material presented, disclose the commission of a cognizable offence. The inquiry does not extend to verifying the truth or veracity of the allegations.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the Magistrate was justified in dismissing the application based on cogent reasons (which involved an assessment of merits) was rejected because the court found that an adjudication on the merits of allegations and a determination of facts as baseless is impermissible at the Section 156(3) stage.
The court held that the Magistrate's power under Section 156(3) is very limited and does not permit an inquiry into the merits of the case, contrary to the appellant's contention.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position that the Magistrate's role is limited to determining if a cognizable offence is disclosed was affirmed by the court.

The court agreed with the High Court's decision to remit the matter back to the Magistrate, stating that it was correct because the initial dismissal involved an impermissible adjudication on the merits of the allegations.
policy_considerations: Once an offence is disclosed, an investigation must necessarily follow in the interest of justice, as it is required for gathering necessary materials for establishing or proving the offence.
Absence of a proper investigation where an offence is disclosed may allow an offender to escape from the consequences, which would be detrimental to the cause of justice and society at large.
